ai_industry.title: I went to a Jev hackathon to find out why the new AI model is taking San Francisco by storm
ai_industry.summary_original: TypeSafe's Jev has taken San Francisco developers by storm and could mark a shift in AI. At a hackathon, engineers rushed to build software with Jev.
ai_industry.content_original:
When a new twist on AI called Jev arrived this month, San Francisco's tech scene responded as it does: lots of hype, and then a hackathon.
Jev is a new and viral AI model built by the startup TypeSafe AI, and developers are flocking to try it out. Jev's launch video from mid-September has racked up almost 40 million views on X, throwing founder Diogo Almeida into the spotlight.
Notably, Jev marks a break from large language models (LLMs) at OpenAI and Anthropic. Rather than spitting out text, Jev makes decisions. It's also dirt cheap and incredibly fast. An ex-OpenAI researcher, Almeida has said that the focus on chatbots doesn't do enough to automate rote work.
I attended a Jev hackathon on Saturday at the startup CodeRabbit's office to find out what the hype is all about. The event became something of a coming-out party for Jev. Some developers say they have already woven Jev into their products and feel that TypeSafe has delivered a true breakthrough. Sourabh Mane, a design engineer at CodeRabbit, called it a "breath of fresh air."
Venture capitalists are buzzing around Jev as well. The Information reports that some VCs have offered to invest in TypeSafe at a $10 billion valuation.
How Jev differs from chatbots like ChatGPT
Jev takes in questions and rapidly responds with structured answers that include probability estimates of accuracy. It works best when engineers break down their questions into the most specific possible pieces, Allie Laabs, TypeSafe's head of developer relations, told the crowd at the start of the hackathon.
Laabs told me that, with Jev, her startup hopes to advance a new school of thought in an industry dominated by LLMs.
"What if this path that we've been so horse-blinders on, the LLM path, what if that's not the only path?" she said.
Laabs gave the developers some other pointers, too. Jev works well for classifying — it could mow through customer support queries and slot them into buckets, or moderate a fast-moving online chat feed. She hopes that Jev's speed and low cost will help some developers build tools they'd previously thought were too ambitious.
Developers sprint to inject Jev into their code
Fueled on croissants and coffee, the developers were thrilled to get going.
Cofounder Jalaja Kurubarahalli said that if Jev can sort questions more quickly, it could reduce the lag in the voice tools that her startup, Quintess AI, builds for maintenance workers. Hitesh Viswasam, a robotics engineer, suggested that a model like Jev could let robots respond to heat or danger at human-like speeds.
Some attendees had already improved their code with Jev. Developer Lawrence Liang showed me the personal AI agent he'd built for himself. He said this was his second Jev hackathon of the week and that he'd built the model into 80% of his agent's code infrastructure. Jev figures out much more quickly than an LLM which tools are needed for any given query.
"It almost blows your mind," Liang said.
Engineer Avram Cheaney said that adding Jev to his AI search product for eBay, called JunkDrawer.ai, had made it "drastically cheaper and drastically faster" than using just LLMs. Those few seconds of speedup are particularly important for consumer products, where people have become used to instantaneous loading.
"This is what's been missing," Cheaney said.
TypeSafe peddles a new way to think about AI
It's been a hectic week at TypeSafe. Jev's launch catapulted the company from anonymity to a closely watched AI player. Its Discord server now has more than 100,000 members.
"It is definitely completely nuts," Laabs said, adding that the early success is something "very few people ever get to experience in their lives."
Laabs said she's been delighted to see that people have quickly begun to understand what Jev can do.
Before, she was worried because Jev doesn't align precisely with how AI is widely understood, where a text box spits out code or detailed answers to questions.
"A software engineer has to put it in something; it isn't anything until that," Laabs said. She's found that the explanation helps: "Then people go, 'Ohhh!'"

ai_industry.title: Modulate raises $25M to sell AI that listens to voice calls, not just transcripts
ai_industry.summary_original: Modulate, a Boston company that builds AI models to analyze speech directly rather than working from text transcripts, has raised $25M in a round led by Future Ventures. Hyperplane and Lakestar also took part, bringing the company’s total funding to $60M. The…
ai_industry.content_original:
Modulate, a Boston company that builds AI models to analyze speech directly rather than working from text transcripts, has raised $25M in a round led by Future Ventures. Hyperplane and Lakestar also took part, bringing the company’s total funding to $60M.
The company was founded by Mike Pappas and Carter Huffman, who first met at MIT when Mike worked out a physics problem that Carter was solving in a hallway. They soon became friends because of their shared interest in how computers affect people’s ability to connect.
“Voice is becoming a primary interface for AI, and that creates a whole new set of problems that can’t be solved from a transcript,” said chief executive and co-founder Carter Huffman, who took over the top job from co-founder Mike Pappas, now chairman.
The main product, Velma, can analyze audio signals, picking up on emotion, tone, intent, emphasis, and whether the voice is synthetic. The various signals can then be combined to identify higher-level events such as a fraud attempt, a harassment case, or a frustrated customer, and this can be done in real time during an ongoing call.
Instead of using one large model, Velma employs what Modulate calls an Ensemble Listening Model, which selects and combines more than 100 smaller, specialized audio models for each task.
The company states that this method is up to 1,000 times more efficient than using a single large model and that Velma is twice as accurate as general-purpose large language models at identifying actual problems while generating seven times fewer false alarms; those comparisons are made by Modulate itself.
Its public benchmark results are easier to check. In July, Modulate’s transcription models took first place out of 88 entries on Hugging Face’s Open ASR Leaderboard, and its deepfake detector has ranked first on Hugging Face’s Speech Deepfake Arena since March, with an equal error rate of 1.1%. Batch transcription costs $0.03 an hour.
The deepfake work lands in a market where cloned voices have become an established tool for fraud. Modulate says hospitals use its models to defend against deepfake callers, and that its systems now process more than 10mn hours of audio a month, with more than 600mn hours analyzed in total. It also offers voice masking to protect staff in high-risk roles and detects child grooming in voice conversations.
Steve Jurvetson, co-founder of Future Ventures, said the company had “gained a significant technical lead in audio-native AI” and that demand was spreading well beyond gaming into AI agents, security, and customer experience.
The money will go into research, engineering, and a push to court developers with new SDKs, APIs, and partner integrations, so that companies building voice products can buy audio understanding rather than train their own models.

ai_industry.content_original:
Instagram is the latest social media platform to add built-in AI-powered features that will give users feedback on their posts. The company announced Wednesday that its standalone Edits app will now include an AI “creative assistant” that pulls in data from a user’s Instagram account and offers suggestions on what to change.
Instagram is adding an AI ‘assistant’ to tell you how to post
What happens when platforms tell everyone how to optimize their content?
Using the new assistant, creators can ask open-ended questions about what’s trending on Instagram, why one video worked and another didn’t, or what piece of content resonated most with their audience. The tool pulls in data and metrics such as likes, views, retention on videos, and shares. Instagram says it can spot patterns over time and give a creator suggestions that metrics alone can’t provide. Creators can also ask for ideas for content, how to hook viewers, what captions to use, which audio tracks are trending, and how to script videos.
Are you a creator using platforms’ AI tools?
I want to hear from you about your experience. Contact me at mia@theverge.com or at miasato.11 on Signal.
If that sounds familiar, it’s because YouTube also just announced updates to its sprawling AI-powered dashboard that tells creators how to maximize engagement. (YouTube’s version, which it initially announced in 2025, also has AI editing and A/B testing capabilities.) If you’ve been online for a while — and especially if you’ve ever had to pay attention to social media metrics — you’ll know that this is quite a shift. Historically, many platforms have limited or even hidden detailed metrics about how your own content is performing. The platforms certainly have not been open about why a video or post performed poorly. Tools like CrowdTangle, which researchers and journalists used to monitor the most popular content on Meta platforms, have been shut down or restricted. Now, both YouTube and Instagram are effectively promising to give creators personalized advice on how to ride the algorithm.
It’s in both the platforms’ and creators’ best interest to shape content for maximum engagement. As I wrote earlier this month, though, what happens when everyone is perfectly optimizing their content? Will content become even more similar as creators adjust to one another? Is there no ceiling for the amount of time audiences are willing to spend on the platforms? The shift also raises interesting new questions about the relationship between tech companies and the creators that fill the platforms with things to look at: How does this dynamic change when platforms are straightforwardly giving creators instructions on how to post?
The new feature is free for creators to use, up to a point. Meta says “power users” will be able to buy a Meta One subscription for more usage. This, too, speaks to the changing winds: Meta needs to finance its lofty AI ambitions, and it’s already signaled that premium social media features may be part of how it does it. It’s not hard to imagine a future where meaningful feedback and AI-driven analytics and insights are for paying subscribers. In the end, it may end up re-creating the same frustrations and opaqueness that have plagued content creators for years — but this time, behind a paywall.
